title: Hormuz on the Brink of Reopening, Every Other Front Escalating
subhead: A week that began with Iran firing ballistic missiles at US forces and ended with Oman-mediated talks on reopening the Strait of Hormuz — the most promising diplomatic breakthrough in five months of war. But on every other front, from Ukraine's deep strikes into Russia to Europe's migration crisis and climate catastrophe, the trajectory was one of escalation, not resolution.

sections.heading: Hormuz: From Blockade to Near-Breakthrough in a Week
sections.body:
The week began with Iran launching 'multiple' ballistic missiles at US forces in the Middle East on Tuesday, shattering a three-day ceasefire lull that had raised hopes of a diplomatic opening. All missiles were intercepted, but the exchange of fire — combined with US-Saudi retaliatory strikes on IRGC sites in eastern Iraq — underscored the cycle of escalation that has defined this conflict since February.

By Sunday, the tone had shifted dramatically. Trump announced he had called off 'the biggest attack since World War II' on Iran after Gulf allies urged de-escalation, claiming deal 'perimeters' had been agreed. Iran denied any direct negotiations, saying it was only talking to Oman about a temporary shipping route. By Monday, the gap between the two sides' public positions was stark: Trump insisted negotiations were happening 'right now'; Iran's Foreign Ministry said nothing significant would change 'as long as the maritime siege continues.'

Then on Tuesday, a breakthrough appeared imminent. Secretary of State Rubio said 'progress has been made' on safe shipping lanes, and Treasury Secretary Bessent told CNBC a deal could come 'today or tomorrow.' The rough outline, per a former Pentagon official: Iran would restrict passage through its territorial waters while allowing free transit through Omani waters — effectively ending the traditional right of innocent passage but keeping commercial traffic flowing. Oil prices dropped sharply, with Brent falling below $80 a barrel for the first time since July 13.

Throughout the week, Iran pushed a new maritime route through Hormuz — separate from existing corridors — that its Foreign Ministry said would 'respect the sovereign rights of both sides.' Ships transiting the strait dwindled to single digits per day, compared with over 100 before the war. Only eight vessels passed on Sunday and 11 on Saturday, according to Kpler data.
sections.whyItMatters: A Hormuz reopening would be the most significant de-escalation since the June MoU, but the pattern of this conflict is lulls followed by collapse. Even if a deal emerges, Iran's proxy networks in Iraq, Yemen, and the Red Sea remain active — and past ceasefire attempts have unraveled within days.

sections.heading: Ukraine Escalates Deep-Strike Campaign as Air Defences Thin
sections.body:
Ukraine dramatically expanded its drone war inside Russia this week, striking targets as far as Udmurtia — over 1,300km from the front line — and repeatedly hitting Wildberries warehouses near Moscow, St Petersburg, and Tver. Kyiv says the online retailer's logistics network supplies the Russian military. A Wildberries warehouse in Samara was completely destroyed. The deep strikes killed at least 14 people in Russia, including seven on a beach in the Krasnodar region and three in Udmurtia.

On the Ukrainian side, the picture was bleaker. Russia fired a record 376 missiles at Ukraine in July, more than double June's total, with most aimed at Kyiv. At least eight people were killed in an overnight barrage on August 1, including five members of the Voronov family near Kryvyi Rih. Three of their children remain missing. A Polish-confirmed Russian Kh-101 cruise missile landed in eastern Poland — manufactured near Moscow in the second quarter of this year, evidence that Russia is burning through newly built stock.

Ukraine's ability to defend itself is eroding. Zelenskyy warned of a critical shortage of Patriot interceptors, saying air defences intercepted 154 drones but only one ballistic missile in the latest barrage. US Patriot stockpiles have fallen from roughly 2,330 before the Iran war to fewer than 827, per CSIS. Trump walked back his promise to license Patriot production in Ukraine, saying 'people that you give that technology, they can some day turn on you.' The Pentagon announced a $58 billion, seven-year contract with Lockheed Martin to triple Patriot production and quadruple THAAD output — but that is a long-term investment, not an immediate fix.
sections.whyItMatters: Ukraine is hitting Russia harder and deeper than ever, but its air defence umbrella is thinning as US interceptors are diverted to the Iran conflict. Trump's reversal on Patriot production for Ukraine, combined with Russia's accelerating bombardment, means Kyiv's ability to protect its cities is deteriorating even as its offensive reach expands.

sections.heading: Ceuta: 75 Dead, Schengen Fractured, 800 Children Stranded
sections.body:
As many as 72,000 people surged across from Morocco into Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta on July 30-31, in the largest single-day migration event to hit a European border in years. By week's end, approximately 70,000 had returned to Morocco, but the death toll stood at 75 on the Spanish side and 11 in Morocco — many drowned attempting the crossing. More than 800 unaccompanied minors remain stranded in Ceuta with limited food and shelter, in a facility designed for 600.

The political fallout was immediate and far-reaching. Italy suspended its Schengen free-movement arrangement with Spain, a move backed by Finland and Denmark. Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš called for Spain's Schengen membership to be temporarily suspended. Spain's PM Pedro Sánchez accused critics of acting from 'prejudice, fake news, ignorance, or political interest,' pointing out that Ceuta is not part of the Schengen zone. Spain installed a 500-metre floating barrier off the coast and allocated 25 million euros for the care of unaccompanied minors.

By Tuesday, EU interior ministers broadly endorsed Spain's handling of the crisis, with EU Commissioner Magnus Brunner calling it a 'test' of European resilience that had been 'passed.' But the underlying fractures remain: 22 EU nations signed a letter of concern, and the precedent of Schengen suspension has been set. The crisis was reportedly triggered by a Spanish Supreme Court ruling barring summary returns of migrants stopped at sea, combined with social media-fuelled disinformation about open borders.
sections.whyItMatters: The Ceuta crisis has set two precedents in a single week: the largest mass crossing into Europe in years, and the first Schengen suspension by a member state targeting another. Even as the immediate influx recedes, the political and institutional damage to Europe's border regime will persist.

sections.heading: The Netanyahu-Trump Rift Goes Public
sections.body:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu held a closed-door meeting with Trump at the White House on Tuesday, but the optics told the story of a deteriorating relationship. Netanyahu entered via a side entrance, no press questions were taken, and the White House offered only that the encounter was 'positive and productive.' Hours before the meeting, Trump publicly told Fox News he didn't need Netanyahu's intelligence on Iran's nuclear sites, adding: 'Frankly, we're being very nice to a lot of countries that would not survive without us. And you know who wouldn't survive without us? Israel.'

Trump also pushed back on Israel's opposition to resuming F-35 sales to Turkiye, and the broader pattern is clear: Washington is charting its own course on Iran, one that may prioritize a diplomatic exit over Israel's preference for continued military pressure aimed at regime change. Netanyahu, facing elections in October, is using his proximity to the White House for domestic political purposes — a dynamic Trump clearly resents.

The friction extends to Gaza, where Israel has expanded its territorial control to over 60 percent of the strip even as a Hamas disarmament deal — brokered through Trump's Board of Peace — was announced on Thursday. Israel has not signed on. Far-right Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir called the plan 'unacceptable,' and Israeli officials insist no withdrawal will occur before full disarmament. Israeli strikes killed at least 13 people in Gaza on Sunday, including several children, even as the disarmament framework was supposed to be taking hold.
sections.whyItMatters: The Trump-Netanyahu relationship — the foundation of the US-Israel military partnership in the Iran war — is fraying in public. While military support continues unchanged, Trump's willingness to overrule Israeli objections on arms sales and publicly rebuff Netanyahu's lobbying signals that US and Israeli interests on Iran are diverging.

sections.heading: Climate Catastrophe Compounds Conflict: Rivers Dry, Fires Rage
sections.body:
Europe's twin crises — wildfire and drought — deepened dramatically this week. In France, a wildfire described by the interior minister as having 'a life of its own' came within 15km of Bordeaux, forcing the evacuation of 220,000 people and destroying 240 homes. Macron called it France's 'toughest wildfire since World War Two.' Over 420 sq km burned in under four days. Four firefighters were killed. In Spain, fires west of Madrid burned 770 sq km — an area larger than the city itself. The Gironde fires generated pyrocumulonimbus — fire-created thunderstorms that produce lightning capable of starting new blazes.

Simultaneously, Europe's major rivers hit record lows. The Rhine fell to its lowest recorded levels at measuring stations in Cologne and Lobith, with 44% of Rhine stations and 78% of Danube stations registering 'extremely low' water levels. The key Kaub chokepoint hit 25cm — matching the 2018 record low — forcing cargo vessels to lighten loads. Serbia cut coal plant output due to cooling water shortages. Romania carried out a controlled explosion on a Danube riverbank rock to maintain water flow to its Cernavoda nuclear plant. Dacia and Ford factories in Romania agreed to halt production for over two weeks to reduce electricity consumption.

The WMO warned that a strengthening super El Niño is pushing global weather into 'uncharted territory,' with Pacific waters warmer than any previous El Niño at this stage. The forecast threatens India's monsoon with below-normal rainfall, endangering food security for over a billion people. France's prime minister revealed that 162 arrests for arson have been made since July 6 — nine out of ten French fires were caused by humans, though climate conditions made them unstoppable.
sections.whyItMatters: The simultaneous drought and wildfire emergency is disrupting shipping, power generation, and agriculture across Europe at precisely the moment Hormuz disruptions are already straining energy logistics. Compounding climate shocks with conflict-driven supply shocks raises the risk of cascading food and energy inflation across the continent.

sections.heading: Currency War: First US-Japan Yen Intervention Since Fukushima
sections.body:
Japan and the United States carried out a rare coordinated currency intervention to halt the yen's plunge to a 40-year low against the dollar. Japan's Ministry of Finance said it sold nearly $59 billion worth of dollars on Thursday, before Friday's joint intervention with the US Treasury — the first coordinated action since the 2011 Fukushima disaster. A Reuters photograph captured Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's handwritten to-do list during a Camp David cabinet meeting: 'Buy Japanese Yen $5-10 bil.'

The dollar fell from around 164 yen to 157.6 within hours. Trump told reporters: 'They have a weakening yen, and they wanted a little bit of help. And we're always there for Japan.' Oxford Economics noted the US participated because a stronger yen reduces Japanese export competitiveness pressure and could ease global financial instability that might push up US borrowing costs — a calculation driven substantially by war-related energy inflation.

The inadvertent disclosure of Bessent's notes was a remarkable breach of financial protocol, raising questions about whether the intervention was coordinated with Japan in advance or represented a unilateral US response to currency pressures amplified by the Iran conflict's effect on oil prices.
sections.whyItMatters: The first joint US-Japan currency action in 15 years signals that the dollar-yen imbalance had reached systemic risk territory. It also reveals how deeply the Iran war's economic ripple effects have penetrated — Washington is now deploying direct currency tools to manage war-driven inflation.

sections.heading: Red Sea: No Safe Alternative to Hormuz
sections.body:
Just as a Hormuz reopening deal appeared imminent, the Red Sea — the supposed alternative route for Middle Eastern oil — suffered its own disruption. An Indian-flagged vessel, the MSV Faize Noore Oliya, was struck by a projectile and sank off the coast of Yemen on Tuesday. All 14 crew members were rescued by the Yemeni coastguard. Yemen's internationally recognized government blamed the Iran-backed Houthis, saying a boat laden with explosives was used in the attack.

The Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia's Red Sea ports on July 20 and have since claimed attacks on oil tankers, commercial shipping, and energy infrastructure — including a drone strike on Najran airport that damaged its main radar system. A Saudi strike on the Houthi-controlled port of Salif killed at least 68 people, according to the Houthi-run health ministry.

The dual blockage of Hormuz and the Houthi campaign in the Red Sea has created what analysts describe as a near-total disruption of Middle Eastern oil export routes. Existing bypass pipelines can handle only about 9 million barrels per day of the 20 million that normally transit Hormuz — and routing traffic through the Red Sea simply moves the vulnerability from one chokepoint to another.
sections.whyItMatters: The sinking of a commercial vessel in the Red Sea underscores that even a Hormuz deal won't restore normal oil flows. With both major export routes from the Gulf compromised, the global energy disruption has no quick fix — making the Hormuz negotiations even more consequential.

sections.heading: Japan Earthquake, Argentina Strike, Pakistan Insurgency: Secondary Shocks
sections.body:
A 6.8 magnitude earthquake struck Japan's Kumamoto prefecture on Tuesday, killing at least 13 people and trapping dozens in a collapsed shopping mall. The Aeon Mall in Kumamoto partially collapsed with three confirmed dead at the site. At the Nippon Paper Industries plant, a chimney collapse left two in cardiac arrest and nine missing. TSMC's Kumamoto semiconductor plant — a strategic asset in the US-China chip competition — reported operations were 'gradually resuming' after confirming structural safety. Some 36,700 households lost power and sections of the 17th-century Kumamoto Castle walls crumbled.

In Argentina, maritime pilots walked off the job after President Milei published a decree deregulating river navigation services. At least 45 vessels are stuck at Argentine ports, with the export chamber warning 30 more ships would be affected each day the strike continues. Argentina is the world's largest exporter of soya bean products, and any prolonged disruption at its Parana River ports ripples through global food markets already stressed by Hormuz and Red Sea shipping crises.

In Pakistan's Swat Valley, a suicide bomber killed 14 people at a police station near an anti-violence rally — a grim irony that underscored the accelerating TTP insurgency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Just days earlier, an ambush using explosive-laden drones killed 11 police officers. Researchers recorded 154 terrorism-related deaths in the province in July alone, more than double June's toll. No group claimed the Swat bombing, but Pakistan has repeatedly accused Afghanistan's Taliban government of sheltering attackers.
sections.whyItMatters: These secondary crises — a semiconductor-threatening earthquake in Japan, a grain port shutdown in Argentina, an intensifying insurgency in Pakistan — illustrate how the world's overlapping vulnerabilities compound each other. Each on its own would be manageable; together, they strain a global system already at capacity.

bottomLine: This week may be remembered as the moment the Iran war's trajectory pivoted — or didn't. A Hormuz reopening deal, mediated by Oman, appears closer than at any point since the June MoU, and oil markets rallied on the prospect. But the fundamentals haven't changed: Iran denies direct talks with the US, Houthi attacks are sinking ships in the Red Sea, and every previous ceasefire in this conflict has collapsed within days. Meanwhile, the war's ripple effects deepened on every other front. Ukraine's air defences are thinning as Patriot stockpiles run low, Trump reversed his promise on domestic production for Kyiv, and Russia is firing newly manufactured missiles into both Ukraine and NATO territory. Europe faces compounding climate and migration crises — 75 dead in Ceuta, record-low rivers, and wildfires that generated their own thunderstorms. The first US-Japan currency intervention since Fukushima revealed how far war-driven inflation has penetrated the global financial system. And from Argentina's grain ports to Pakistan's Swat Valley, secondary shocks piled onto an already overloaded agenda. The connective thread: every major development this week was an escalation of an existing trend, not a new beginning. The question is whether next week's Hormuz deal — if it materializes — will finally break the pattern, or become the latest cycle of hope and collapse.
sources: Al Jazeera, AP, BBC, Reuters, AFP, Financial Times, Axios, Dawn, CSIS, Kpler, World Meteorological Organization, Saudi Press Agency, NYT, Guardian
